blocks.text: Markets are heterogeneous. The STP approach identifies potential customers, selects which to pursue and formulates the value proposition – focusing resources, building loyalty and increasing profitability.
Post-demographic segmentation: traditional demographics lose predictive power because people construct their own lifestyles and identities.
A segmentation study runs in four phases:
children: I Planning & design: objectives, resources, constraints
II Qualitative assessment: database review, qualitative research, deep needs, decision-making process
III Quantitative measurement: sample design, questionnaire, data collection
IV Analysis & implementation: cluster analysis, cluster profiling, implementation via direct marketing, social media, promotions

blocks.text: Segmentation bases (variables that form segments) differ from descriptors (variables that profile and reach them). The choice depends on the segmentation objective.

Cluster analysis groups consumers so that distances within clusters are minimal and distances between cluster centroids maximal. Test robustness by splitting the sample randomly and re-running the analysis.

children: Structural characteristics: competition, saturation, protectability, environmental risk
Product-market fit: fit with strengths and image, relationships with other segments, profitability

blocks.text: Select target segments with the GE/McKinsey matrix (segment attractiveness × company strengths): weight drivers, rate segments, multiply, plot, run sensitivity analysis. Strong position in highly attractive segments → build preemptive position; weak position in unattractive segments → exit.
Positioning is what you do to the mind of the prospect (Ries & Trout). Differentiation creates differences; positioning makes them distinct, relevant and sustainable in customers' minds.
Positioning analysis has seven steps: target segment, competitive offerings, differentiator dimensions, customer ratings, perceptual map, integrate preferences/choice/share, positioning statement.
Perceptual maps show distances between brands along a few quantifiable dimensions; brand association maps show the network of associations around a brand.
A group of customers who have similar needs and show similar behaviour or lifestyle.
The process of identifying and grouping consumers into relatively homogeneous segments based on shared needs, characteristics, attitudes or behaviours.
Variables used to segment a market; they tell us why segments differ and respond differently.
Characteristics that help profile each segment and reach it with dedicated offerings and communication.
A statistical method that groups consumers based on a series of variables so that members of a cluster are similar and different from other clusters.
A set of strategies a company develops to differentiate its offering in the minds of its target customers.
Techniques that visualise the competitive structure of a market as perceived by customers.

Cluster tables are a classic exam exercise (shopping centre mock exam). Practise: least satisfied cluster, focus aspects, cluster descriptions, attractiveness rating, and recognising when the GE/McKinsey matrix cannot be applied.
